draft.title: Health and longer lives
card: In the 20th century, people in many countries came to live much longer. Better medicine and public health were two main reasons.
Antibiotics
medicines that treat infections caused by bacteria. Illnesses that once often killed people, such as some lung infections, could now often be cured.
Vaccines
given to prevent disease before a person is infected. The polio vaccine, used widely from the 1950s, protected children from a disease that could cause paralysis.
Public health
Clean drinking water, sewage systems and health campaigns lowered the spread of disease. Fewer babies and children died, which helped raise life expectancy.
draft.remember: Antibiotics, vaccines and public health helped people live longer in the 20th century.

a.q: What does a vaccine such as the polio vaccine do?
opts: Protects a person from a disease before they catch it
Cures a person who already has a bacterial infection
Cleans the water supply that a town depends on
Replaces the need for any other health measures
a.why: A vaccine prepares the body so a person is protected before infection. Curing a bacterial infection is the job of antibiotics, which is the tempting wrong option.
a.clue: Vaccines work before a person gets sick.

b.q: A town builds a sewage system and a clean water supply, and fewer children die of disease. Which idea does this best show?
opts: Public health measures can help people live longer
Antibiotics are the only cause of longer lives
Vaccines have no effect on how long people live
Longer lives came only from new hospital buildings
b.why: Clean water and sewage lower the spread of disease, so more children survive and people live longer on average. Antibiotics also helped, but the card does not say they were the only cause, so the word only makes that option wrong.
b.clue: The town changed water and sewage, not medicines.

a.best: Protects a person from a disease before they catch it

b.best: Public health measures can help people live longer

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged claim ('can help'). Every wrong option is an absolute ('only', 'only', 'no effect'), so a student can pick the answer by ruling out the extreme wording without understanding public health.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate. In question b, the right answer is the only option without an absolute word like 'only' or 'no effect', so students can guess it from the wording alone.

a.q: What does a vaccine such as the polio vaccine do?
opts: Protects a person from a disease before they catch it
Cures a person who already has a bacterial infection
Cleans the water supply that a town depends on
Treats a person's symptoms once they are already ill
a.why: A vaccine prepares the body so a person is protected before infection. Curing a bacterial infection is the job of antibiotics, which is the tempting wrong option.
a.clue: Vaccines work before a person gets sick.

b.q: A town builds a sewage system and a clean water supply, and fewer children die of disease. What best explains the fall in deaths?
opts: Disease spread less, so fewer children caught it
Antibiotics cured more children of bacterial infections
Vaccines protected more children before infection
Hospitals gave sick children faster treatment
b.why: Clean water and sewage are public health measures. They lower the spread of disease, so fewer children are infected in the first place. Antibiotics and vaccines also saved lives, but the town changed its water and sewage, not its medicines.
b.clue: Look at what the town actually changed.
